en: He entered alone and attacked.
Humming, he pays no heed.
The great lords and giants,
The spearmen and heroes,
He does not rate as high as his trouser hem.
He did not panic or fall into grief.
When we drew our bows like rain,
When we fired shots like hail,
That bastard blood-drinker of yours,
That deceiver who ruins the world,
Did not so much as move his brow.
Taking a painted spear in his hand,
Your Burut was a champion;
He gripped it at the middle and swung it.
Your Burut was a champion;
The surging army,
He scattered its tumult to dust
And broke its ranks apart.
When he bends down, he spears a hero;
We wholly despaired of life.
He spears many in a row with one thrust.
Men died exchanging blows.
At that fiercely wrathful Burut's hands,
All who faced him died.
He laid the village headmen low.
All who attacked,
He cut and crushed, leaving them stiff.
To drive us back this way,
The blood-drinker surged forward in frenzy.
The forty households in Altay,
Those people you told us to raid,
Escaped and went away unharmed.
‘Collect tribute,’ you sent us.
We went for tribute and lost what we had;
The heroes caught between
We let fall to the lion.
Far from tribute, they gave not a shit.
The forty households went to their homeland.
With the help of Manas,
All the Burut escaped
And migrated to their people.
The young falcon went to its homeland;
Your subjects wandering bewildered,
Those wanderers went to their people.
Our eyes beheld Manas.
He is blue-maned, he is a lion;
No man can bend him down and conquer him.
He is one of exceptional fortune.
We too began a slaughter;
We too killed men.
We came unable to seize the Burut's
Elders Akbaltay and Jakyp.
Powerless, we let them escape,
All forty households.
Unable to obtain your tribute,
We were left stiff between them.
Meeting a formidable lion,
We suffered slaughter, left standing alone.
All the mighty giants were butchered.
On the mighty giants' flesh
Crows and ravens feasted.
All the level ground became dust,
All the hollows became blood.
If that blood-drinker goes on like this,
No strength can overcome him in a struggle.
Even if, meaning to seize him, it bites and gnashes,
A lion's teeth cannot pierce him.
We had failed to take heed.
He is a boy born in Altay.
When we consider it, Khan Esen,
He is trouble born for Beijing.
If that blood-drinker grows furious,
He can bring havoc.
If he charges in and attacks,
He can break into your treasury.
Of the seething Chinese,
He can learn how numerous the people are.
Your Chinese people of forty clans,
He can drive and scatter like crows.
He can seize your crown and wear it,
He can seize your throne and mount it.
Driving all the Chinese,
He can herd them toward Great Beijing.
He can destroy the idol first.
We saw this bearing of the Burut,
Who can bring mighty havoc.
If you gather strength anew,
If in fury you muster an army,
If you gather plenty from all forty khans,
The people will die, the khans will die.
The fierce-wrathed blood-drinker—
Every soul who provokes him will die.
No mortal can bend him down and defeat him;
No one can face him.
If you survive, you will see
That Manas's spectacle,
Upon Kakan-Chin's Beijing,
The fierce havoc he brings.
The reason he brings slaughter—
He is a dark, blue-maned lion,
The whole world, beyond Beijing,
He is a hero who can drive and rule.
None can match him with a sword;
No mortal can defeat him with a spear.
His appearance is unlike a mortal's.
If he lives, upon Beijing
The bold one will bring misery.
He is a lion who came to the Burut;
No such hero exists in the world.
He will not let the plow turn.
That bastard Burut
Will not let us stay in Beijing.
If we grapple and fight,
If we wage a fierce battle,
He will not let the yoke-pins be readied,
Will not let a pair of oxen be yoked,
Will not let the earth's face be opened,
Will not let a handful of seed be sown.
I have spoken grave words; wait and see.
No such son will arise from the Chinese.
There is the time when Khan Manas was born;
For Kakan's vast people,
There is this dark hour.
He is a warrior, he is a lion,
A hero born unlike others.
His fortune is complete.
When we look within him,
It is wider than the face of the earth!
Khan Esenkan, hear my words:
I will not turn and go back,
I will not wage war against Manas!
I will not approach such a blood-drinker,
I will not encounter that deceiver.
Seeing his fury, I suffered;
I despaired of my bare life.
Manas, whose menace is fierce—
Somehow find a way to his mind.
If you are angry, Esenkan,
The four khans who returned alive,
Strike off their heads now!”
Before Esenkan,
Ezkara and Zholoy, the two khans,
What they knew and understood,
What they heard and saw,
Told him in this way.
Having heard them, Esenkan—
His gate was firmly closed;
The khan lost his senses.
Of that vast Burut people,
When their people were overwhelmed and slaughtered,
Their grandfather Karakan,
When he had been watched closely,
When many of his people were slaughtered,
When his daughter was taken as booty,
A great magician from Beijing,
As he scrutinized the people,
One saying of the great magician,
A foul saying that stained the heart—
These were the great magician's words:
‘Seize their great men,’ he said.
‘All their great men,
Slaughter them together,’ he said.
‘If you leave the Burut alive,
Your work is incomplete.
Among those Burut will be born
A child bringing ill fortune.
No man can bend him down and take him.
No one can face him.
He will herd white deer as cattle,
He will confound the peoples of the world.
If Manas is born, he will stir trouble.
His name will be Manas, a hero;
Any who grapple with him will fall short.’
He described Manas's appearance:
‘His face like oiled wheat,’ he said,
‘His eyes like twilight mist,’ he said.
‘A broad mouth, a cliff-like brow—
Such will his appearance be,’ he said.
When of Manas, may your life depart,
I heard the renowned account,
My collarbone gave a jolt,
My heart leapt and quaked.
My knees bent to the ground.
The sixty-leaf chronicle
I brought at a run.
That he would go in fury and venom,
That ill-omened blood-drinker,
I knew he would drink blood.
If Manas should be born,
‘He will make trouble,’ I kept saying.
His onslaught was long known.
‘If blood-drinking Manas is born,
He will bring an onslaught on Kakan’—
Six years earlier, then,
It was inscribed in the book.
I have sorcerers, I have seers;
Receiving word from me,
Not one remained; they rode out.
‘The blood-drinking Burut in the end,
Of Kakan-Chin and Beijing,
Will seize the khanate,’ it said,
‘Will bring havoc,’ it said.
Of this Beijing where we stand,
It was entered in the register.
‘Find Manas and bring him,’ I said.
I gathered my people together,
I sent many of my giants,
I lavished all my livestock,
I had many cities searched.
Without delay I gathered them,
The Chinese elders skilled in discernment,
I had them travel and examine
All the Muslims.
Sending them from city to city,
All those many places
I had searched with the discerning men.
My gold and gold coins,
The henchmen I had sent
Sold and squandered, filling themselves.
With this, the Burut
They ceased to search for.
Falsely saying, ‘This is Manas,’
Puffed out like something stuffed in a sack,
They drove here a man of straw.
One who could do nothing,
They drove here their worthless one.
One who dared not step outside at night,
They drove here their coward.
One who would not walk even when led,
They drove here their calf.
Trusting the magicians,
Our pit had been dug.
Our words lay wasted on the plain;
Our eyes had been blinded!
How have we put Beijing to rights?
That bastard blood-drinker,
We raised him in this Altay.
This Jakyp who was driven here—
Is he not a resourceful enemy?
The wandering, wretched Jakyp,
The Chinese slaughtered his father.
This must be the scheming one,
A cunning man, an enemy within!
His son's name was Chong Zhindi.
That bastard Burut's
Stratagem—who knew of it?
That bastard Jakyp,
Sowing grain and digging ore,
Quietly lived like a poor wretch.
Rumors spread, so they said:
Slaughtering livestock like a king,
Holding a feast for all the people,
‘If my son grows up safely,
He will wage war on Kakan,’ he said.
He had found his means.
